intro.label: Overview
intro.heading: Cane Corso vs Great Dane: The Quick Answer
intro.html:
Both are large Molosser-derived breeds with impressive physical presence. The decisive practical differences: size (Great Dane is 30-80 lbs heavier), temperament purpose (Dane is gentle-giant family dog; Corso is active working guardian), protective instinct (Corso has working-guardian temperament; Dane is famously friendly with strangers), and handling demands (Dane is moderate; Corso requires experienced handling).

For family-pet purposes, Great Dane is the dramatically easier match despite its size. For households specifically wanting a serious guardian, Cane Corso is the right answer.

Last updated May 2026 - by Kailun Zhang

quick_answers.label: Quick Answers
quick_answers.heading: 5 Questions Most People Ask First
quick_answers.html:
Short answers to the questions most people ask before comparing these two:

Q: Which is bigger?

A: Great Dane, by a wide margin. The AKC lists male Great Danes at 140-175 lbs and 30-32 inches tall. Cane Corsos are 'only' about 88-110 lbs, with males 25-27.5 inches.

Q: Which is more protective?

A: Cane Corso. Great Danes will often bark at intruders and their size alone deters, but they are not guardian-bred and are typically friendly with strangers. Cane Corsos retain working-guardian instincts.

Q: Which lives longer?

A: Cane Corso, by 1-3 years (9-12 vs Dane's 7-10). The Dane's enormous size drives shorter lifespan via cardiac, orthopedic, and cancer risk.

Q: Which is better for first-time owners?

A: Great Dane. The calm temperament is more forgiving than the Corso's intensity. Cane Corso is genuinely an experienced-owner breed.

Q: Can either live in an apartment?

A: Great Dane can, given enough floor space - 45-60 minutes of daily exercise plus indoor lounging usually works. Cane Corso is a much harder fit: it needs 60-90 minutes of daily exercise and, ideally, a securely fenced yard.

temperament.label: Personality
temperament.heading: Temperament: Gentle Giant vs Working Guardian
temperament.html:
Great Dane: gentle, friendly, calm indoors

The Great Dane 'gentle giant' reputation is accurate. Modern Danes are calm, patient with children, friendly with strangers, and often sedate indoors (though they still need daily exercise). Not natural guardians - their size is a deterrent but their temperament is not protective.

Cane Corso: reserved, watchful, working drive

Cane Corsos retain working-guardian temperament. They are deeply bonded to family but reserved bordering on suspicious with strangers. Require active engagement (60-90 min daily exercise + mental work).

health.label: Health
health.heading: Health: Both Below-Average Lifespan
health.html:
Great Dane main risks

Bloat/GDV - Purdue studies put Great Danes' lifetime risk at roughly 37-42%, the highest of the breeds studied. Prophylactic gastropexy is standard. DCM at elevated rates. Wobbler's syndrome. Lifespan averages 7-10 years.

Cane Corso main risks

Hip dysplasia. Bloat/GDV. Entropion and ectropion (eyelid abnormalities). Lifespan averages 9-12 years.

mikes_take.label: Personal Take
mikes_take.heading: What I'd Tell a Friend Choosing Between These Two
mikes_take.html:
A first-time owner's take

The honest pitch for each: Great Dane is what you choose if you want a 175-pound dog who behaves like a 30-pound dog - calm, patient, content to lounge. Cane Corso is what you choose if you want a 100-pound dog who behaves like a 150-pound working partner - reserved, watchful, with you when you work.

The mistake is buying either expecting the other. Great Dane buyers who wanted a guardian end up with a friendly couch potato. Cane Corso buyers who wanted a family pet end up with a dog that refuses to settle when company visits. Pick the temperament you actually want.

mistakes.label: Common Mistakes
mistakes.heading: Mistake Index: Buyer Errors to Avoid
mistakes.html:
These are the most common buyer mistakes Wooffy sees come up repeatedly in owner forums and rescue intake stories. Knowing them ahead of time is the cheapest way to avoid years of regret.

Mistakes new Cane Corso owners often make

  • Buying as a first dog or 'cool-looking big dog'. Cane Corsos need experienced handling - calm, consistent structure, early socialization, and ongoing training into adulthood.
  • Inadequate fencing and prey drive management. Corsos have high prey drive including cats, rabbits, and small dogs. A 4-foot fence is not enough.
  • Skipping professional training by age 12 weeks. Corsos test boundaries throughout adolescence (8-24 months). Without structured training, behavioral issues compound.
  • Buying from breeders who don't temperament-test. Quality Corso breeders evaluate puppy temperament before placement. A breeder who lets you 'pick the cute one' is skipping a step that matters with a guardian breed.

Mistakes new Great Dane owners often make

  • Choosing the biggest puppy or heaviest line. Across breeds, bigger dogs tend to live shorter lives, and the AKC standard already puts males at 140-175 lbs. Bigger than standard is not better - ask what the adults in a breeder's line typically weigh.
  • Skipping prophylactic gastropexy. A large prospective study estimated Great Danes' lifetime GDV risk at about 42%. Prophylactic gastropexy at spay/neuter prevents life-threatening gastric torsion. $300-$800 once.
  • Not budgeting for the cardiac reality. DCM is common in the breed - a UK screening study found it in about a third of the Great Danes examined. Regular echocardiogram screening, on the schedule your vet recommends, can catch it before symptoms appear.
  • Underestimating food costs. Adult Great Danes eat far more than a typical large dog, and annual food cost commonly runs $1,000-$2,500 depending on the diet.
  • Inadequate vehicle for transportation. Most sedans are a tight fit for an adult Great Dane; many owners end up needing an SUV, minivan, or other vehicle with room for a giant crate.

breeder_vetting.label: Breeder Vetting
breeder_vetting.heading: How to Vet a Breeder for Either Breed
breeder_vetting.html:
Both breeds have committed reputable breeders and a wide pool of backyard breeders with no health testing. The questions below separate the two.

Ask any Cane Corso breeder

  1. OFA (or PennHIP) hip and OFA elbow certificates for both parents, plus OFA patella results.
  2. OFA cardiac clearance on both parents, and DNA results for NCL and DSRA (both on the breed's current CHIC list).
  3. CAER eye exam on both parents - especially entropion screening.
  4. Temperament evaluation methodology - how do you assess puppies before placement?
  5. Can I see the dam interacting with strangers, kids, and other dogs?
  6. What is your puppy-back policy if the dog develops aggression issues?

Ask any Great Dane breeder

  1. OFA (or PennHIP) hip, OFA thyroid, and eye exam results for both parents (the Great Dane Club of America's recommended clearances).
  2. OFA cardiac clearance with current echocardiogram.
  3. Do you recommend prophylactic gastropexy at spay/neuter?
  4. How old are the grandparents and what were their causes of death?
  5. What is the typical adult weight range in your line? (Within the standard is the goal - bigger is not better.)
  6. Has Wobbler syndrome (cervical instability) shown up in your line?

Red flags - walk away if you see any of these

  • Breeder says "we don't test because our line is healthy".
  • Markets Cane Corso as a "family pet" without temperament evaluation requirements.
  • Encourages pushing a Great Dane puppy's growth with extra calories or calcium supplements (excess calcium and rapid growth are linked to skeletal problems in giant-breed puppies).
  • Will not show you parents in person.
  • Charges premium for "European bloodline" without documentation.
  • Sells puppies before 8 weeks old.

decision.label: Decision
decision.heading: Which Should You Choose?
decision.html:
Choose Great Dane if you...

Want a gentle giant that is often calm indoors. Have space for a 110-175 lb dog. Are emotionally prepared for the 7-10 year lifespan. Want a friendly-with-strangers breed.

Choose Cane Corso if you...

Are an experienced large-breed owner. Want an active guardian. Don't have small pets. Have a secure yard. Are committed to ongoing training.

faq.a: Neither breed is inherently dangerous with proper training and socialization. Corso's higher prey drive and reactive temperament makes incidents more likely with poor training.

faq.q: Can a Great Dane really live in an apartment?
faq.a: Surprisingly yes in many cases. Danes may seem sedate indoors, but they still need 45-60 minutes of daily exercise - AKC suggests a brisk walk two or three times a day - plus indoor lounging.
Different dimensions. Great Dane wins on height (tower-like). Cane Corso wins on muscular density.

faq.q: Do Great Danes really get bloat that often?
faq.a: Yes. In major U.S. veterinary studies, Great Danes had the highest GDV risk of the breeds analyzed - Purdue estimates put the lifetime risk at roughly 37-42% without preventive measures.

faq.q: What about Mastiff or Rottweiler as related options?
faq.a: Worth considering. See Mastiff vs Cane Corso and Rottweiler vs Cane Corso.
